object.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 14 minutes at 14 frames a second, 260 metres, with painted sets and in-camera effects
object.description: Six astronomers are fired from a giant cannon in a bullet-shaped shell, land in the eye of the Man in the Moon, fight the Selenites with umbrellas, and fall back to Earth to a hero's welcome. Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician who had bought a projector in 1896, made it in his glass-walled studio at Montreuil over the summer of 1902, playing the lead astronomer himself and painting the cardboard Moon. At fourteen minutes and thirty tableaux it was the longest and most expensive film he had attempted, and it was his biggest success, sold worldwide and pirated almost at once in the United States by Thomas Edison's agents. The shot of the shell stuck in the Moon's eye has become the emblem of early cinema. Méliès's business collapsed in the 1910s; he burned many of his negatives and ended up selling toys at the Gare Montparnasse before he was rediscovered and honoured in 1929. A hand-coloured print, found in Barcelona in 1993, was restored in 2011.
facts: Loosely based on Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) and H. G. Wells's The First Men in the Moon (1901).
Méliès used stop-substitution, dissolves and painted perspective; the Moon's approach was done by moving the camera on a trolley toward a painted face.
Edison's company copied the film and sold it in America without paying Méliès a cent, a loss he complained of all his life.
The film was added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2002, its centenary year.
